text: Cabell Calloway III (December 25, 1907 – November 18, 1994) was an American jazz singer, songwriter, and bandleader who became a prominent figure in the swing era through his regular performances at the Cotton Club in Harlem. He gained acclaim for blending jazz and vaudeville, a career that spanned over 65 years. A master of energetic scat singing, Calloway led one of the most popular dance bands in the United States from the early 1930s to the late 1940s, featuring trumpeters Dizzy Gillespie, Jonah Jones, and Adolphus "Doc" Cheatham, saxophonists Ben Webster and Leon "Chu" Berry, guitarist Danny Barker, bassist Milt Hinton, and drummer Cozy Cole. He achieved several hit records in the 1930s and 1940s, becoming the first African-American musician to sell one million copies of a record, with his most famous song, "Minnie the Moocher," originally recorded in 1931. This song earned him the nickname "The Hi-de-ho Man" and was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame in 1999 and added to the Library of Congress' National Recording Registry in 2019. Calloway reached the Billboard charts in five consecutive decades (1930s–1970s). He made numerous stage, film, and television appearances, including roles in Stormy Weather (1943), Porgy and Bess (1953), The Cincinnati Kid (1965), and Hello Dolly! (1967), and experienced a career resurgence in the 1980s with his appearance in The Blues Brothers (1980). He was the first African-American to have a nationally syndicated radio program and received the National Medal of Arts from the U.S. Congress in 1993. He posthumously received the Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award in 2008. Born in Rochester, New York, on December 25, 1907, Calloway's father, Cabell Calloway Jr., graduated from Lincoln University of Pennsylvania in 1898, and his mother, Martha Eulalia Reed, was a Morgan State College graduate, teacher, and church organist who also worked as a lawyer and in real estate. The family moved to Baltimore, Maryland, in 1919, where Calloway grew up in the West Baltimore neighborhood of Druid Hill. He skipped school to earn money by selling newspapers, shining shoes, and cooling down horses at the Pimlico racetrack, where he developed an interest in racing and gambling. After being caught playing dice on the church steps, he was sent to Downingtown Industrial and Agricultural School in 1921. Upon returning to Baltimore, he resumed hustling and worked as a caterer while improving his education. He began private vocal lessons in 1922 and studied music throughout his schooling. Despite his parents' and teachers' disapproval of jazz, he began performing in nightclubs in Baltimore, with mentors including drummer Chick Webb and pianist Johnny Jones. He joined his high school basketball team and played professionally with the Baltimore Athenians in the Negro Professional Basketball League during his senior year, graduating from Frederick Douglass High School in 1925. He briefly attended law school in Chicago before leaving to pursue a singing career. In 1927, he joined his older sister, Blanche Calloway, on tour for the revue Plantation Days, whom he credited as his inspiration for entering show business. After the tour ended, he enrolled at Crane College in Chicago but refused an opportunity to play basketball for the Harlem Globetrotters to pursue singing. He performed at "Black and tan" clubs such as Chicago's Dreamland Café, Sunset Cafe, and Club Berlin, where he was an understudy for Adelaide Hall and met Louis Armstrong, who taught him scat singing. He left school to join the Alabamians band. In 1929, the band opened at the Savoy Ballroom and, after the Alabamians disbanded, Armstrong recommended Calloway to join the musical revue Connie's Hot Chocolates, where he established himself as a vocalist singing "Ain't Misbehavin'" by Fats Waller. When the Missourians asked him to front their band in 1930, they became known as Cab Calloway and His Orchestra. In 1931, the band was hired at the Cotton Club in Harlem to substitute for Duke Ellington, leading to a permanent position. The band performed twice a week for NBC radio broadcasts, and Calloway appeared on programs with Walter Winchell and Bing Crosby, becoming the first African American to have a nationally syndicated radio show. During the Great Depression, he earned $50,000 a year at age 23. In 1931, he recorded "Minnie the Moocher," the first single by an African American to sell a million copies. He performed the song and others, "St. James Infirmary Blues" and "The Old Man of the Mountain," in the Betty Boop cartoons Minnie the Moocher (1932), Snow-White (1933), and The Old Man of the Mountain (1933), providing voice-over and using rotoscoping to base the characters' movements on his dance steps. The success of "Minnie the Moocher" made him known as "The Hi-de-ho Man." He appeared in a series of short films for Paramount, where his and Ellington's groups were featured more than any other jazz orchestras of the era. In these films, he performed a gliding backstep dance move, described by some as a precursor to Michael Jackson's moonwalk, which he called "The Buzz" in later years. The 1933 film International House featured his song "Reefer Man," about a man who smokes marijuana. Fredi Washington was cast as his love interest in Cab Calloway's Hi-De-Ho (1934), and Lena Horne made her film debut as a dancer in Cab Calloway's Jitterbug Party (1935). In 1936, he made his first Hollywood feature film appearance opposite Al Jolson in The Singing Kid, singing several duets with Jolson and featuring Calloway's band and 22 Cotton Club dancers. Film critic Arthur Knight noted that the film reflected a shift in American culture through Calloway's rhythmic and melodic singing style. In 1938, he released Cab Calloway's Cat-ologue: A "Hepster's" Dictionary, the first dictionary published by an African American, which became the official reference book of the New York Public Library. A revised version was released in 1939 with Professor Cab Calloway's Swingformation Bureau, and the final edition, The New Cab Calloway's Hepsters Dictionary: Language of Jive, was published in 1944. Poet Lemn Sissay stated in a 2014 BBC documentary that Calloway was taking ownership of language for a people whose languages had been taken away. His band included notable musicians such as Ben Webster, Illinois Jacquet, Milt Hinton, Danny Barker, Doc Cheatham, Ed Swayze, Eddie Barefield, and Dizzy Gillespie. Calloway recalled that he expected precision in his musicians, as he built songs around scat or dance steps. The band formed baseball and basketball teams, playing each other and local semi-pro teams, and participated in charity games. In 1941, he fired Dizzy Gillespie after a fracas when Calloway was hit with spitballs; he wrongly accused Gillespie, who stabbed Calloway in the leg with a small knife. From 1941 to 1942, he hosted a weekly radio quiz show called The Cab Calloway Quizzicale, a parody of Kay Kyser's The College of Musical Knowledge. During World War II, he entertained U.S. troops before they departed overseas. The band recorded songs with social commentary, including "Doing the Reactionary," "The Führer's Got the Jitters," "The Great Lie," "We'll Gather Lilacs," and "My Lament for V Day." In 1943, he appeared in Stormy Weather, one of the first mainstream Hollywood films with a black cast, featuring Bill "Bojangles" Robinson, Lena Horne, the Nicholas Brothers, and Fats Waller. He hosted Horne's character Selina Rogers as she performed the title song in a big all-star revue for soldiers. In 1946, he published a humorous pseudo-gossip column called "Coastin' with Cab" for Song Hits magazine. In the late 1940s, poor financial decisions and gambling led to the breakup of his band. In 1956, his daughter Lael and he recorded "Little Child," an adaptation of "Little Boy and the Old Man," which charted on the Billboard Hot 100. In 1958, Lee Sherman was the choreographer for The Cotton Club Revue of 1958, which starred Calloway and featured tap dancing prodigies Maurice Hines and Gregory Hines. That year, he released the album Cotton Club Revue of 1958 on Gone Records, produced by George Goldner and conducted and arranged by Eddie Barefield. In 1958, he appeared in St. Louis Blues, the life story of W.C. Handy, featuring Nat King Cole and Eartha Kitt. The Cotton Club Revue of 1959 toured South America, visiting Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo, and also stopped in Uruguay and Argentina before returning to North America, including a Broadway run. He remained a household name through TV appearances and concerts in the U.S. and Europe, touring with the Harlem Globetrotters in 1961 and 1962 for halftime entertainment. In 1965, he appeared in The Cincinnati Kid with Steve McQueen, Ann-Margret, and Edward G. Robinson. He performed on The Ed Sullivan Show on March 19, 1967, with his daughter Chris Calloway. In 1967, he co-starred with Pearl Bailey as Horace Vandergelder in an all-black cast of Hello, Dolly! on Broadway, with Chris Calloway joining as Minnie Fay, reviving the show's business and leading to a rare RCA Victor cast recording. In 1973–74, he was featured in an unsuccessful Broadway revival of The Pajama Game with Hal Linden and Barbara McNair. His autobiography, Of Minnie the Moocher and Me, was published in 1976, including his complete Hepster's Dictionary as an appendix. In 1978, he released a disco version of "Minnie the Moocher" on RCA Victor that reached the Billboard R&B chart. He appeared in The Blues Brothers (1980), introducing him to a new generation. In 1985, he and his Orchestra performed at The Ritz London Hotel for a 60-minute BBC TV show, with Adelaide Hall, Doc Cheatham, Max Roach, and the Nicholas Brothers also appearing. A performance with the Cincinnati Pops Orchestra in August 1988, directed by Erich Kunzel, was recorded and featured a classic rendition of "Minnie the Moocher," 57 years after its original recording. In January 1990, he performed at the Meyerhoff Symphony Hall with the Baltimore Symphony. That year, he made a cameo in Janet Jackson's music video "Alright." He continued performing at jazz festivals, including the New Orleans Jazz & Heritage Festival and Greenwood Jazz, and in 1992 embarked on a month-long tour of European jazz festivals. He was booked to headline "The Jazz Connection: The Jewish and African-American Relationship" at New York City's Avery Fisher Hall in 1993 but withdrew due to a fall at home. In January 1927, he had a daughter named Camay with Zelma Proctor. His daughter was one of the first African Americans to teach in a white school in Virginia. He married his first wife, Wenonah "Betty" Conacher, in July 1928; they adopted a daughter named Constance and divorced in 1949. He married Zulme "Nuffie" MacNeal on October 7, 1949. The family lived in Long Beach on the South Shore of Long Island, New York, bordering Lido Beach, and in the 1950s moved to Westchester County, New York, where he and Nuffie raised their daughters Chris Calloway (1945–2008), Cecilia "Lael" Eulalia Calloway, and Cabella Calloway (1952–2023). Calloway was an Episcopalian. In December 1945, he and friend Felix H. Payne Jr. were beaten by police officer William E. Todd in Kansas City, Missouri, after attempting to enter the whites-only Pla-Mor Ballroom to visit bandleader Lionel Hampton. They were hospitalized and charged with intoxication and resisting arrest, but the charges were dismissed. When Hampton learned of the incident, he refused to continue the concert. Todd claimed they refused to leave and struck him, but Calloway and Payne maintained they were sober; six civil rights organizations, including the NAACP, demanded Todd be fired, though he had already resigned after a pay cut. In 1952, Calloway was arrested in Leesburg, Virginia, on his way to a race track in Charles Town, West Virginia, charged with speeding and attempted bribery of a policeman. On June 12, 1994, Calloway suffered a stroke at his home in Westchester County, New York, and died five months later from pneumonia on November 18, 1994, at the age of 86, at a nursing home in Hockessin, Delaware. A memorial service was held.

On June 12, 1994, Calloway suffered a stroke at his home in Westchester County, New York, and died five months later from pneumonia on November 18, 1994, at the age of 86, at a nursing home in Hockessin, Delaware. A memorial service was held at Cathedral of St. John the Divine. He was survived by his wife, who died in 2008, five daughters, and seven grandsons, and was buried at Ferncliff Cemetery in Hartsdale, New York. Music critics have noted his influence on later entertainers such as James Brown, Michael Jackson, Janet Jackson, and modern-day hip-hop performers. John Landis, who directed Calloway in The Blues Brothers, stated, "Cab Calloway is hip-hop." Timothy White wrote in Billboard (August 14, 1993): "No living pathfinder in American popular music or its jazz and rock 'n' roll capillaries is so frequently emulated yet so seldom acknowledged as Cabell 'Cab' Calloway. He arguably did more things first and better than any other band leader of his generation." In 1998, the Cab Calloway Orchestra, directed by Calloway's grandson Chris "CB" Calloway Brooks, was formed. In 2009, Big Bad Voodoo Daddy released an album titled How Big Can You Get?: The Music of Cab Calloway. In 2012, Calloway's legacy was celebrated in a PBS American Masters episode titled "Cab Calloway: Sketches." In 2019, plans were announced to demolish Calloway's boyhood home at 2216 Druid Hill Avenue in Baltimore, replacing it and the block with Cab Calloway Legends Park. Family members and the National Trust for Historic Preservation advocated for preservation due to its significance as an African-American cultural heritage site. Although the block is designated "historically significant" on the National Register of Historic Places, Baltimore City officials stated at a July 9, 2019 hearing that the Calloway house and adjacent properties have "extensive structural damage." The Commission on Historical and Architectural Preservation's executive director noted that properties in worse condition than the Calloway House have been restored with city tax credit support. Maryland Governor Larry Hogan urged the demolition be postponed to allow for preservation as a historic house museum, similar to the Louis Armstrong House in New York. Design options for Cab Calloway Square included an archway from the facade as part of the entrance, proposed by architects working with Baltimore City and the Druid Heights Community Development Corporation. Despite objections, the house was razed on September 5, 2020. In 1985, Town Supervisor Anthony F. Veteran declared a "Cab Calloway Day" in Greenburgh, New York. In 1990, Calloway received the Beacons in Jazz Award from The New School in New York City, and New York City Mayor David Dinkins proclaimed the day "Cab Calloway Day." In 1992, the Cab Calloway School of the Arts was founded in Wilmington, Delaware. In 1994, Calloway's daughter Camay Calloway Murphy founded the Cab Calloway Museum at Coppin State College in Baltimore, Maryland. The New York Racing Association (NYRA) annually honors Calloway, a native of Rochester, New York, with a stakes race for New York-bred three-year-olds as part of their New York Stallion Series. First run in 2003, The Calloway has undergone various distance and surface changes and is currently run at Saratoga Racecourse in Saratoga Springs, New York. The race celebrated its 13th renewal on July 24, 2019, and was won by Rinaldi. In 2020, Calloway was inducted into the National Rhythm & Blues Hall of Fame. Calloway received accolades in positions and features, including short subjects.
